evidence_classes.derived: arithmetic over measured inputs with no free parameters (calibration bins, the CAL threshold sweep, per-sample router paths under a frozen tau)
evidence_classes.estimated: a modeling assumption the reader is invited to move (c_misroute, c_human, the Tier A amortized-zero compute charge) — never a measurement
evidence_classes.measured: read off a real observation: a logged run metric, a per-call receipt, or a deterministic derivation from a frozen per-example artifact
evidence_classes.projected: an extrapolation to conditions not evaluated (e.g. cost at a volume no run reached); carries the assumption that produced it
evidence_classes.provenance: a self-reported coursework result, copied verbatim from the read-only seed archive under docs/seed-evidence/ — NOT verified or reproduced by this lab; provenance, not evidence

paragraphs: A three-tier consumer-complaint triage lab on the CFPB Consumer Complaint Database: TF-IDF linear models (Tier A), fine-tuned transformers (Tier B) and Claude LLMs via OpenRouter (Tier C), combined into a confidence-cascade router optimized against an explicit business cost model and stress-tested against measured 2015 to 2026 distribution drift.

55 append-only run records back this page. Every headline number carries a 95% bootstrap confidence interval (1,000 resamples, fixed seed 20260805) and a reproduction command, and traces to results/runs.jsonl or to a committed derived artifact.

paragraphs: Tier A is a word+char TF-IDF logistic regression with isotonic calibration: macro-F1 0.7605 [0.7564, 0.7643] on the frozen TEST-IID slice, n=104,443.

Fine-tuning buys a certified but modest gain. ModernBERT-base scores 0.7878 / 0.7878 / 0.7863 macro-F1 across the three frozen seeds, and the paired B1 minus A delta is +0.0273 [+0.0234, +0.0312] — an interval that excludes zero.

The pre-registered surprise was CONFIRMED. DistilBERT — the smaller, cheaper deployment point — reaches 0.7950 [0.7909, 0.7988] and tops every ModernBERT seed: the paired B1 minus B2 delta is -0.0072 [-0.0106, -0.0038] with McNemar p=6.3e-08.

Zero-shot LLMs land between the two learned tiers on quality and far above both on price. Haiku 4.5 scores 0.7697 [0.7499, 0.7886] on TEST-IID at a measured $1.315/1k calls; Sonnet 5 scores 0.7418 [0.7015, 0.7730] on its paired 1,500-row subsample at $3.659/1k. Supports differ by point and are not comparable as populations.

On the rows both LLMs scored, the bigger model buys nothing in distribution. Paired on the same 1,500 TEST-IID complaints, Sonnet minus Haiku is -0.0073 [-0.0427, +0.0263] macro-F1 with McNemar p=1.00 — statistically tied, at nearly three times the measured price per call. That tie does not survive drift; the next section is where it breaks.

paragraphs: Tier A walks down and then falls off a cliff. Its yearly macro-F1 goes 0.7579 to 0.7478 to 0.7295 to 0.6656 [0.6585, 0.6729] from 2023 to 2026-H1, on frozen slices of n=20,000 each.

It dies of both wounds. Against the 2023 reference the loss decomposes as total +0.0924 [+0.0802, +0.1042] = prior shift +0.0420 [+0.0385, +0.0454] plus within-class degradation +0.0503 [+0.0385, +0.0625]. The credit_reporting F1 goes 0.9000 to 0.2147.

Tier B2 has the same shape at a smaller magnitude: 0.7901 to 0.7262 [0.7193, 0.7326] yearly; total +0.0639 [+0.0536, +0.0751] = prior +0.0303 [+0.0266, +0.0337] + within +0.0336 [+0.0234, +0.0451]; the prior share is 0.4744 [0.3876, 0.5689] against Tier A's 0.4549 [0.3950, 0.5237], intervals that overlap. Its credit_reporting F1 goes 0.9082 to 0.2853. The pre-registered “B2 behaves like an LLM under drift” hypothesis is REFUTED: fine-tuning bought loss magnitude, not loss shape.

One comparison is certified rather than directional. B2's within-class damage is smaller than Tier A's: the paired within_A minus within_B2 delta is +0.0168 [+0.0058, +0.0276] on the same n=20,000 rows with identical bootstrap draws, and the interval excludes zero (robust across decomposition paths). The certification covers evaluation-sample uncertainty only — Tier B2 is a single fine-tune from one seed, so this is a statement about these two fitted systems, not about the model families.

The LLMs pay only the prior penalty. Haiku's prior component is +0.0305 [+0.0145, +0.0438] while its within-class component is -0.0227 [-0.0651, +0.0193], an interval containing zero. At the cliff the four points are Tier A 0.6656, Tier B2 0.7262, Haiku 0.7278 and Sonnet 0.7821.

That last gap is where the two LLMs stop being interchangeable, and the paired evidence for it comes from a different frozen slice — TEST-POSTCUTOFF, whose boundary sits strictly after both models' training cutoffs. On the same 1,500 rows there, Sonnet minus Haiku is +0.0458 [+0.0282, +0.0663] macro-F1 with McNemar p=2.0e-10, after the two were statistically tied on TEST-IID. The capability gap only shows up off the training distribution: in distribution you are paying for it and not collecting it. (The 2026-H1 points above are un-paired slice metrics, not that comparison — different slice, different claim.)

paragraphs: The escalate-to-human rate under the frozen CAL threshold is flat for four years — 0.0947, 0.1032, 0.0993, 0.1003 from 2022-H2 through 2025, against a CAL operating point of 0.0994 — and then jumps to 0.1674 [0.1623, 0.1724] at 2026-H1, a relative rise of 67%.
The escalate-to-DistilBERT arm under the same frozen gate moves 0.2962, 0.3161, 0.3034, 0.3292 over the same slices and then 0.4849 [0.4780, 0.4921], a rise of 47%.
The gate is doing real work exactly where it is needed: at 2026-H1 the answered set scores accuracy 0.7436 [0.7365, 0.7502] against 0.6918 [0.6858, 0.6982] on the full slice.

But the frozen-threshold cascade slightly trails the un-gated DistilBERT at the same cliff — system accuracy 0.7550 [0.7488, 0.7610] against 0.7584 [0.7526, 0.7647]. That is threshold staleness: a gate fitted on CAL self-adjusts late and abruptly rather than degrading gracefully, which is a monitoring requirement, not a tuning bug.
sections.title: Frozen thresholds go stale late and abruptly

paragraphs: The headline router is a confidence gate in front of Tier A with DistilBERT as the terminal, evaluated on the full TEST-IID slice under cost-model v2 (Tier B priced by an amortized ESTIMATE, not a measurement). It is the only certified two-axis win in the study: against a DistilBERT-only baseline it is both cheaper, -$21.49 [-$26.14, -$16.66] per 1k complaints, and better, macro-F1 +0.0025 [+0.0010, +0.0042] — both paired intervals exclude zero.
In absolute terms it runs at $812.83 [$800.94, $824.90] per 1k at system macro-F1 0.7976, dominating Tier A alone ($933.41), ModernBERT alone ($862.60) and DistilBERT alone ($834.32).

The same gate in front of Tier A alone buys -$60.60 [-$66.79, -$54.88] per 1k and +0.0870 [+0.0841, +0.0899] system macro-F1 against un-gated Tier A. The gate is certified in front of DistilBERT too, but it is worth far less per 1k there. What pays is not the gate; it is routing to cheap capacity.

The cheapest policy measured is the two-gate cascade that ends at Haiku: $786.10 [$729.67, $843.74] per 1k on the paired 5,000-row subset. But its edge over DistilBERT alone is NOT established: -$25.10 [-$53.94, +$4.93], an interval containing zero.

paragraphs: Under 10% character corruption on TEST-IID, the word+char Tier A model loses -0.0436 [-0.0469, -0.0403] macro-F1 to typos while the word-only sensitivity arm loses -0.0661 [-0.0697, -0.0626]. The char-n-gram block therefore absorbs roughly 34% of the typo damage — a directional read only: the two arms are different fitted models with independently bootstrapped intervals and no joint CI was computed. The case family is an exact structural zero for Tier A, +0.0000 [+0.0000, +0.0000], because both TF-IDF blocks lowercase their input; it is reported as an end-to-end control on the plumbing, not as a robustness finding.

Haiku loses least. On the same 1,500 paired rows its typo delta is -0.0310 [-0.0480, -0.0161], while ocr +0.0115 [-0.0081, +0.0317] and case +0.0031 [-0.0188, +0.0258] are both null — their intervals contain zero. The cross-tier ranking under character noise is LLM at least as robust as word+char TF-IDF, and both ahead of word-only TF-IDF.

Robustness carries a serving-cost tax that quality metrics do not show. On those same rows, corrupted text inflates Haiku's prompt tokens by 7.9% (typo), 2.8% (ocr) and 8.8% (case). The case family has the largest inflation and no measurable quality effect at all — noisy inputs make escalation more expensive exactly when Tier A is least reliable.
sections.title: Robustness has a price even when quality holds

paragraphs: The out-of-vocabulary explanation was REFUTED. Model-vocabulary token OOV moves only from 0.545% on TRAIN to 0.773% at 2026-H1, and the TF-IDF centroid distance PEAKS in 2025 at 0.0926 [0.0909, 0.0951] and FALLS at 2026-H1 to 0.0815 [0.0801, 0.0833] — disjoint intervals. Lexical drift is ruled out; the cliff is prior shift. Types and tokens tell opposite stories: 53.4% of TYPES at 2026-H1 are outside the model vocabulary, against 0.773% of TOKENS.

The few-shot hypothesis was REFUTED. On the same 1,500 CAL rows, Haiku with k=9 exemplars scores 0.7674 [0.7351, 0.7986] against 0.7567 [0.7217, 0.7891] at k=0, for double the measured spend ($3.92 against $1.96). Paired on those rows the delta is +0.0107 [-0.0054, +0.0266] macro-F1, McNemar p=0.41 — an interval containing zero. The exemplars bought no measurable quality for twice the money, so every Tier C final in the study is zero-shot.

The LLM cascade does not pay. Under the primary operating point the Haiku-terminal cascade is cheaper than Tier A alone, -$22.76 [-$41.96, -$2.37] per 1k, but it buys no established quality: macro-F1 +0.0070 [-0.0027, +0.0165], an interval containing zero, so the two-axis claim is not certified. Head to head against the gate-to-human router on the same 5,000 rows it resolves AGAINST the cascade: +$47.74 [+$22.53, +$74.74] per 1k, more expensive with the interval excluding zero.

items.text: Not a production serving system. There are no SLA, throughput or uptime claims; latency was bench-measured (and through OpenRouter), never fleet-measured.
Single-domain and English-only: US consumer-finance complaints. Generalization to other triage domains is not demonstrated.
Tier C costs are point-in-time prices for specific model IDs, recorded per call. Forward cost claims are projected, and the frontier is a method, not a leaderboard.

The business cost-model parameters — misroute cost, human-review cost and the Tier B amortized compute price — are ESTIMATED defaults, not measurements. Their sensitivity is exposed in the policy-builder panel rather than asserted away.
LLM contamination on pre-cutoff data is possible. It is mitigated by TEST-POSTCUTOFF (a boundary strictly after the latest Tier C training cutoff), not eliminated.
CFPB narratives are opt-in and CFPB-scrubbed, so there is selection bias against the full complaint population; the scrubbing artifacts are in-distribution quirks the models learn from.
No online learning and no human-in-the-loop feedback were measured, and the escalation arm assumes humans are always right — a modeling choice, stated as one.

The coursework seed scores that motivated this lab are self-reported class results: provenance, not evidence. The group NER project was collaborative, so role attribution there is biographical context, not a measured claim.

caveats: The NER project was group work. Role attribution — that the owner led the modeling — is biographical context, not a measured claim, and nothing in this archive verifies it.

The coursework datasets (Reuters, CoNLL-2003) are research-licensed and were deliberately excluded from this repo. Only the write-ups are archived; no coursework dataset, notebook or submission file is redistributed here.
gaps: The upgrade plan's appendix cites a best Kaggle public score of 0.83615, from a later submission whose only record is a notebook docstring that is NOT in this archive. The page quotes what the committed session summary states — the best of the four submissions it documents — and treats the higher figure as uncited.

The same appendix frames the NER progression from a starter-code baseline of 0.8136, which comes from a document that is not in this archive either. The page therefore starts the progression at the owner's own first phase, which the committed summary does state.
The 'coursework could not afford bootstrap CIs' line traces to the group's presentation speaker notes, which are not in this archive. It is stated as narrative lineage, not quoted as a source.

The plan's general caveat says both coursework reports acknowledge AI assistance. In the committed archive, the Naive Bayes report carries an explicit acknowledgement section, while the NER summary instead documents a feature catalogue synthesized from AI research sources. The page says what the files say.

items.text: The from-scratch multinomial Naive Bayes report (Reuters, five news classes): tokenizing, Porter stemming, frequency-based feature selection, Laplace smoothing, log-space scoring and a macro-F1. This is the ancestor of this lab's classical tier — which is sklearn, not this code.

Per-document Naive Bayes predictions at 3000 selected features — the smallest sweep setting. The report's sweep row for this setting was scored from this file; it is kept as the output artifact behind a quoted number, not as a number itself.

Per-document Naive Bayes predictions at 5000 selected features — a sweep setting. The report's sweep row for this setting was scored from this file; it is kept as the output artifact behind a quoted number, not as a number itself.

Per-document Naive Bayes predictions at 10000 selected features — the assignment's required setting. The report's sweep row for this setting was scored from this file; it is kept as the output artifact behind a quoted number, not as a number itself.

Per-document Naive Bayes predictions at 15000 selected features — the largest sweep setting. The report's sweep row for this setting was scored from this file; it is kept as the output artifact behind a quoted number, not as a number itself.

The dated iteration log of the CoNLL-2003 MEMM NER project (group work): four feature phases with dev scores, four Kaggle submissions each with a stated hypothesis and a stated verdict, harmful features identified and removed with reasons, an out-of-memory failure and its fix. Its lesson list is what this lab's method section was built from.

A crawl-and-preprocess pipeline over 200 scraped book descriptions, from the earliest coursework project. The upgrade plan's reuse-versus-discard audit discarded that project outright: nothing in it seeds this lab, and it is archived here only so the citation set is the whole archive rather than the flattering part of it.

lineage.lesson: Convergence is a hyperparameter, not a detail: raising the MEMM's MAX_ITER from 15 to 25 was the single biggest gain in the NER project, bigger than any feature it tried.
lineage.practice: Every training and optimization constant lives in a per-run YAML config whose hash is stamped into the run record, so no result depends on a value nobody wrote down.

lineage.lesson: Removing harmful features beat adding good ones — no_gaz and pl|s3 were dropped with mechanistic explanations, and the score moved.
lineage.practice: Negative results are first-class: EXPERIMENT_LOG.md publishes the failed hypotheses, and this page's 'what this does not prove' section is as long as its results.

lineage.lesson: Each Kaggle submission changed exactly one thing against the previous one, so every score delta had a candidate cause.
lineage.practice: Single-variable experiment discipline: one config delta per run, one appended record in results/runs.jsonl, one logged verdict.

lineage.lesson: The dev-to-test drop of about 0.04 F1 was diagnosed as a temporal out-of-vocabulary gap between news periods, and reported as structural rather than explained away as noise.
lineage.practice: The entire drift protocol: yearly evaluations, the prior-shift decomposition, and OOV tracking against the frozen training vocabulary.

lineage.lesson: The coursework could not afford bootstrap confidence intervals and said so in its own presentation notes, which left every improvement claim resting on a single point estimate.
lineage.practice: This lab puts a bootstrap interval on every headline number and a paired interval on every comparison claim; a delta whose interval contains zero is reported as a tie.

paragraphs: This lab began as the rewrite of three graduate NLP coursework projects, and the figures in this section are here for lineage only: coursework seed scores are self-reported class results — provenance, not evidence. No claim anywhere else on this page rests on them. Everything this lab asserts rests instead on artifacts a stranger can re-derive: a frozen CFPB snapshot, an append-only run log, a bootstrap interval on every headline number, and a reproduction command for each one.

The numbers below were copied character-for-character out of docs/seed-evidence/, a read-only citation archive of the original write-ups. They were not recomputed and have not been verified here; the build simply refuses to print a figure it cannot find in the archived file. The Naive Bayes report also carries an explicit AI-assistance acknowledgement, and the NER project's feature catalogue was synthesized from AI research sources — which is one more reason the portfolio narrative rests on this lab's evidence rather than on these.

Naive Bayes on the five-class Reuters set, implemented from scratch: macro-F1 0.9647679093041557 at the required 10000-feature setting, over 5,787 training and 2,298 test documents. Sweeping the feature count across 3000 / 5000 / 10000 / 15000 moved the score only between 0.9636702838478547 and 0.9658523189692165 — a spread with no interval around it, which is exactly the habit this lab was built to break.

The MEMM NER project logged four documented feature phases, from a dev macro-F1 of 0.8322 to 0.8733, and four Kaggle submissions between 0.82335 and 0.83522, each with a stated hypothesis and a stated verdict — including one recorded, in the summary's own words, as HYPOTHESIS WRONG. That summary also calls its dev-to-test gap of about 0.04 F1 a structural property of the corpus: the test split comes from a later period of news with a higher out-of-vocabulary rate. A drift protocol grew out of that sentence.
